question: According to reports, electricity theft in Greece has reached alarming proportions, with the total cost to the electricity market estimated at hundreds of millions of euro annually. This cost appears to be passed on indirectly to honest consumers through electricity tariffs, burdening households and small businesses.

At the same time, numerous complaints from citizens have been recorded about arbitrary or incompletely documented electricity theft charges by the Hellenic Electricity Distribution Network Operator (HEDNO), which have led to legal appeals, with several decisions in favour of consumers.

In the same context, the Regulatory Authority for Waste, Energy and Water (RAAEY) has imposed an administrative fine on HEDNO for the violation of prescribed procedures and abusive practices in the control of and imposition of charges for electricity theft.
Given the obligations of the Member States to protect consumers, ensure transparency in the operations of network operators and ensure fair cost sharing in the internal energy market: 1.
How does the Commission assess the passing on of the costs of electricity theft to honest consumers in light of EU law on consumer protection and transparency in the energy market?

Does the Commission consider practices of imposing electricity theft charges by network operators to be compatible with EU law, when they are not based on fully documented, transparent and verifiable controls?

Does the Commission intend to request information from Greece and to examine the need for additional guidelines or supervisory measures, thus ensuring that tackling electricity theft does not lead to an unjustified burden on honest consumers?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.4.2026) EU law requires Member States to ensure transparent, cost-reflective and non-discriminatory network charges. Article 18(1) and (7) of Regulation (EU) 2019/9431 require that network tariffs reflect the costs of an efficient operator and are applied transparently.

Electricity theft may be reflected in non-technical losses; however, under Articles 18(2) and 18(8) system operators must provide incentives to boost efficiency, thereby also implying the reduction of losses. It is for national regulatory authorities (NRAs) to ensure that tariff methodologies comply with these principles.

Directive (EU) 2019/9442 establishes consumer protection requirements, notably as regards bills and billing information (Article 18, Annex I), basic contractual rights (Article 10) and access to effective dispute resolution mechanisms (Article 26).

While EU law does not provide specific provisions or harmonise national procedures for establishing electricity theft, Member States must ensure that practices applied by network operators comply with the framework set out in the Directive. It is for national regulatory authorities to monitor compliance, address complaints and ensure appropriate redress, without prejudice to national courts.

The Commission continues to monitor the implementation of EU electricity legislation. At this stage, the Commission notes that NRAs and national courts are better placed to address electricity theft while safeguarding transparency and consumer protection.
